title: AI Regulation and Compliance: The EU AI Act and Beyond
subtitle: Work out which AI rules apply to your systems, what they require of providers and deployers, and how to build a compliance programme that keeps up as the rules are phased in.
outcomes: Explain why AI is regulated, and how the EU AI Act's risk-based approach and staged application work
Identify whether your organisation is a provider, a deployer or another operator for each AI system
Classify AI systems as prohibited, high-risk, subject to transparency duties or minimal risk, and list the obligations that follow
Apply the rules for general-purpose AI models, and the transparency duties, to products built on them
Connect the AI Act with the GDPR, the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001, and plan a compliance programme
prerequisites: No legal training is needed, but it helps to know how AI systems are built or bought, and the basics of data protection. The course explains the law so you can work well with your legal and compliance advisers; it isn't legal advice.
description: The EU's AI Act, which the EU describes as the first comprehensive legal framework on AI anywhere, reaches organisations well beyond Europe: any that place AI systems on the EU market, or whose systems' outputs are used there. This course explains what it requires and how to comply, in plain language. You'll learn why AI is regulated, how the Act defines an AI system, and how its risk-based approach and staged timeline work. You'll work out your organisation's role for each system, recognise the practices the Act bans, decide whether a system is high-risk and list what providers and deployers must then do. You'll apply the rules for general-purpose AI models, and the transparency duties for chatbots, generated content and deep fakes, to products built on those models. Then you'll connect the Act with the GDPR and with frameworks used around the world, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001, and plan a compliance programme from inventory to monitoring. Because the Act's obligations apply in stages, and some dates may be adjusted, you'll also learn where to check the current official timeline. The labs are classification and drafting exercises on realistic scenarios, and the course ends with a compliance plan for a fictional company.

modules.title: Why AI is regulated, and the EU AI Act's approach
modules.summary: The risks that lead governments to regulate AI, the AI Act's scope, definition, risk-based approach and staged application, and the roles it gives organisations.

lessons.title: Why AI is regulated
objectives: Explain the risks that lead governments to regulate AI
Describe how existing laws already apply to AI
key_points: Governments regulate AI because some uses can harm health, safety and fundamental rights, such as privacy and non-discrimination, in ways that are hard for people to see or challenge.
AI strains existing rules: its decisions can be opaque, systems can change after deployment, and responsibility is spread across developers, suppliers and users.
Existing laws already apply to AI, including data-protection, consumer-protection, non-discrimination and product-safety laws, and sector rules such as those for finance and medical devices.
AI-specific laws aim to give businesses legal certainty and people protection and, in the EU's case, one set of rules across the single market instead of different national laws.

Approaches differ: some jurisdictions have comprehensive AI laws, others rely on existing regulators and sector rules, and many publish voluntary principles, so check each place you operate, as the rules change quickly.

lessons.title: The EU AI Act at a glance
objectives: Describe the AI Act's scope, its definition of an AI system and its risk-based approach
Explain how its obligations apply in stages, and where to check the current timeline
key_points: The AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, entered into force on 1 August 2024; as a regulation, it applies directly in every EU member state without national laws to transpose it.

It defines an AI system as a machine-based system that operates with some autonomy, may adapt after deployment, and infers from its inputs how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions.

It covers providers placing AI on the EU market wherever they're based, deployers in the EU, and those elsewhere whose systems' output is used in the EU; it excludes military, defence and national-security uses, pure research and personal non-professional use.

Its risk-based approach bans a few practices, sets detailed requirements for high-risk systems, adds transparency duties for some others and leaves most AI, such as spam filters, without new obligations; general-purpose AI models have their own rules.

It applies in stages: the bans and AI literacy duties first, from February 2025, then the rules for general-purpose AI models from August 2025, with most other obligations, including for high-risk systems, later; the EU has proposed moving some later dates, so check the official timeline.

Fines for prohibited practices can reach 35 million euros or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, with lower ceilings for other breaches; for SMEs and start-ups the lower of the two amounts applies.

walkthrough.title: Check the official text and timeline

steps.do: Go to EUR-Lex, the EU's official website for its law (eur-lex.europa.eu), and search for 2024/1689.
steps.see: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act, available in every official EU language.

steps.do: Open the text and find Article 113, Entry into force and application, which sets out when each part of the Act applies.
On the regulation's page, look for later amending acts and for a consolidated version that includes them: an amendment can change dates and obligations.
Visit the European Commission's AI Act pages on its digital strategy website (digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu) for guidelines, codes of practice and the latest news on timing.
Write down the date you checked and what you found, and set a reminder to check again, because guidance and timings are still being added and adjusted.

lessons.title: Roles: providers, deployers and others
objectives: Identify an organisation's role for each AI system it makes or uses
Explain when a deployer or distributor becomes a provider
key_points: A provider develops an AI system or general-purpose AI model, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark, whether for payment or free.
A deployer uses an AI system under its authority in a professional activity, such as a bank using a credit-scoring system bought from a vendor; personal, non-professional use doesn't count.
Importers, distributors and authorised representatives have their own, lighter duties, mainly checking that a system carries the required marking and documentation before passing it on.
One organisation can hold different roles for different systems, such as provider of the chatbot it built and deployer of the recruitment tool it bought.

A deployer, distributor or importer becomes the provider of a high-risk system if it puts its name or trademark on it, makes a substantial modification, or changes a system's intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk.
Roles drive obligations: providers carry most duties for high-risk systems, while deployers must use them as instructed, oversee them and inform the people affected.

lab.title: Build an AI inventory and identify roles
lab.goal: For a fictional company's six uses of software, decide which are AI systems under the AI Act and what the company's role is for each.
setup: A document or a sheet of paper
The scenario: a mid-sized logistics company based in the EU, with the six uses listed in the first step

steps.do: Read the company's six uses of software.
steps.code:
U1. A customer-service chatbot on its website, which it built on a general-purpose AI model from another company, accessed through an API, and offers under its own brand.
U2. A CV-ranking tool, bought from a vendor, that its HR team uses to shortlist job applicants.
U3. The spam filter in the email service it subscribes to.
U4. A demand-forecasting model its data team built for planning warehouse staffing.
U5. A spreadsheet that calculates overtime pay using fixed rules written by the payroll team.
U6. A fleet-tracking product it sells to other firms under its own brand, which now includes a delay-prediction module licensed from an AI vendor.

steps.do: For each use, decide whether it's an AI system under the Act's definition, and give your reason in one line. Write it as AI system: yes or AI system: no.
For each AI system, name the company's role (provider, deployer or both) and any other organisation's role, such as the vendor that provides a system or the company that provides a model.
Note any use where the company has more than one role, and any where another organisation's documentation will be essential for the company's own compliance.
List two questions you'd ask the company to confirm your answers, such as how a system is described in its contract.

checks.text: U5 is identified as not an AI system, because it only applies rules written by people.
U2 and U3 make the company a deployer, with the vendors as providers.
U1, U4 and U6 make the company a provider: U1 and U6 under its own brand, and U4 put into service for its own use.
U1 notes that another company provides the general-purpose AI model, and U6 that the module's vendor supplies a component.
Two questions to confirm the answers are included.

lab.submit: Paste your inventory: for each of U1 to U6, the AI system line, the roles with reasons, your notes on multiple roles and documentation, and your two questions.
hints: Putting an AI system into service for your own use counts: a company that builds a model for its own operations is its provider.
The definition centres on inference: a system that only follows rules people wrote, with no learning or inference, isn't an AI system.

modules.title: Prohibited practices and high-risk systems
modules.summary: The practices the AI Act bans, how to tell whether a system is high-risk, and what providers and deployers of high-risk systems must do.

lessons.title: Prohibited practices
objectives: List the AI practices the AI Act prohibits
Recognise the narrow exceptions
key_points: Article 5 bans AI that uses subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques, or exploits vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a social or economic situation, to distort people's behaviour in ways that cause or are likely to cause significant harm.

It bans social scoring: evaluating or classifying people on their social behaviour or personal traits where the score leads to unjustified or disproportionate detrimental treatment, or to treatment in unrelated contexts.

It bans predicting that a person will commit a crime based solely on profiling or personality traits, and building or expanding facial recognition databases by untargeted scraping of images from the internet or CCTV.

It bans emotion recognition in workplaces and education institutions, except for medical or safety reasons, and biometric categorisation that infers race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation.

Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement is banned except in narrowly defined cases, such as searching for victims of serious crimes or preventing an imminent terrorist threat, with prior authorisation.
The bans have applied since 2 February 2025, carry the Act's highest fines, and the European Commission has published guidelines with examples of what they do and don't cover.

lessons.title: What makes a system high-risk
objectives: Apply the two routes by which an AI system becomes high-risk
Use the Annex III areas and the exception for systems that don't pose a significant risk
key_points: An AI system is high-risk if it's a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the EU product laws listed in Annex I, such as those on machinery, toys, lifts or medical devices, and the product needs a third-party conformity assessment.

It's also high-risk if it's used in an area listed in Annex III: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, access to essential services, law enforcement, migration and border control, and justice and democratic processes.

Annex III examples include ranking job applicants, deciding promotions or monitoring workers' performance, assessing creditworthiness, pricing life and health insurance, admitting students and evaluating learning outcomes.

An Annex III system isn't high-risk if it doesn't pose a significant risk of harm, for example when it only performs a narrow procedural task or a task preparatory to a human assessment; but a system that profiles people is always high-risk.
A provider that decides an Annex III system isn't high-risk must document that assessment before placing the system on the market, and register it.
The Commission can update the Annex III list, and the Act asks it to publish guidelines with practical examples of high-risk and other uses, so check for current guidance.

lessons.title: Obligations for high-risk systems
objectives: List what providers of high-risk systems must do
List what deployers of high-risk systems must do
key_points: Providers must run a risk management system across the life cycle, use training, validation and test data that meet quality criteria, keep technical documentation and build in automatic logging.
Their systems must come with clear instructions for use, be designed for effective human oversight, and achieve appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity.

Before placing a system on the market, the provider carries out a conformity assessment, draws up an EU declaration of conformity, affixes the CE marking and registers Annex III systems in the EU database.
Providers also need a quality management system, post-market monitoring, and procedures to take corrective action and report serious incidents to the authorities.

Deployers must use the system as instructed, give human oversight to people with the competence and authority for it, monitor its operation, keep its logs and report serious risks or incidents to the provider and authorities.

Deployers must tell people when a high-risk system makes or helps make decisions about them; public bodies and some others, such as deployers of credit-scoring systems, must first assess the impact on fundamental rights.

lab.title: Classify AI systems under the AI Act
lab.goal: Classify eight AI uses as prohibited, high-risk, subject to transparency duties or minimal risk, citing the relevant article or annex, and name the role of the organisation using each.
setup: A document or a sheet of paper
The text of the AI Act on EUR-Lex (search for 2024/1689), to look up Article 5, Article 6, Article 50 and Annex III

steps.do: Read the eight scenarios.
steps.code:
S1. A company uses software that analyses employees' facial expressions in video meetings to rate how engaged they are.
S2. A recruitment platform ranks job applicants' CVs and recommends whom to interview.
S3. A bank's model scores loan applicants' creditworthiness.
S4. An online shop's chatbot answers customers' questions about their orders.
S5. An email service's spam filter.
S6. A university's system marks exam answers, and the marks count towards degrees.
S7. A firm scrapes photos from social media to build a facial recognition database it sells to clients.
S8. A tool that only sorts incoming job applications into folders by the job applied for, without assessing the applicants.

steps.do: For each scenario write one line: its number, its category (prohibited, high-risk, transparency duties or minimal risk) and the article or annex point you rely on.
For each high-risk system, say who would usually be the provider and who the deployer, and list three obligations for each of them.
For S8, explain which Annex III area it falls in and why the exception in Article 6(3) may apply, and what the provider must do if it relies on it.
For S4, write the first message the chatbot could show to meet its transparency duty.

checks.text: S1 (emotion recognition at work) and S7 (untargeted scraping for facial recognition) are prohibited under Article 5.
S2, S3 and S6 are high-risk under Annex III: employment, creditworthiness and education.
S4 falls under the transparency duties in Article 50, with a first message that says customers are talking to an AI.
S5 is minimal risk, with no new obligations.

S8 is in the employment area of Annex III, but the Article 6(3) exception for narrow procedural tasks may apply, provided it doesn't profile people; the provider must document the assessment and register the system.
The roles and obligations for the high-risk systems name both providers and deployers.

lab.submit: Paste your eight classification lines, the roles and obligations for each high-risk system, your S8 explanation and the S4 chatbot message.
hints: Emotion recognition is banned in workplaces and education unless it's for medical or safety reasons; rating engagement in meetings is neither.
Creditworthiness assessment is high-risk, but AI used only to detect financial fraud is excluded from that point of Annex III.

modules.title: General-purpose AI and transparency
modules.summary: The rules for general-purpose AI models, what changes when you build a product on someone else's model, and the transparency duties for chatbots, generated content and deep fakes.

lessons.title: General-purpose AI models
objectives: Explain what a general-purpose AI model is under the AI Act
List the obligations of their providers, including for models with systemic risk
key_points: A general-purpose AI model shows significant generality and can competently perform a wide range of distinct tasks, such as a large language model, however it's released; the rules for these models have applied since 2 August 2025.

All their providers must keep technical documentation, give downstream providers the information they need to use the model in their own systems, have a policy to comply with EU copyright law and publish a summary of the content used for training.
Models released under a free and open-source licence with their weights made public are exempt from the documentation duties, unless they pose systemic risk.

A model is presumed to have systemic risk when its training used more than 10²⁵ floating-point operations, or when the Commission designates it; its provider must also evaluate it, including adversarial testing, reduce systemic risks, report serious incidents and ensure cybersecurity.

The General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, published in July 2025, gives providers a voluntary way to show they meet these obligations, and the Commission's AI Office supervises general-purpose AI models.

lessons.title: Building on general-purpose AI models
objectives: Work out your role when you build a product on another company's model
Plan what to ask a model provider for
key_points: A company that builds an AI system on a general-purpose model accessed through an API, and offers it under its own name, is the provider of that AI system, even though another company provides the model.
A system's risk category depends on its intended purpose, not on the model: the same model can power a minimal-risk writing aid and a high-risk CV-screening tool.
Downstream providers rely on the model provider's documentation to meet their own obligations, so ask for it, with information on capabilities, limitations and acceptable uses.
Modifying a model, for example by fine-tuning it, can make you a provider with obligations covering your modification; the Commission's guidelines on general-purpose AI explain when.
Contracts with model providers should cover how your data is used, security, incident reporting, notice of changes to the model, and support for your own compliance.

lessons.title: Transparency obligations
objectives: Apply the transparency duties to chatbots, generated content and deep fakes
Write disclosures that meet them
key_points: Providers must design AI systems that interact directly with people so that people are told they're dealing with an AI system, unless that's obvious from the context.

Providers of systems that generate synthetic audio, images, video or text must mark the outputs in a machine-readable format, so they can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated, as far as technically feasible.

Deployers who make deep fakes, AI-generated or altered images, audio or video resembling real people, objects, places or events that could falsely seem authentic, must disclose it; for evidently artistic or satirical work, a disclosure that doesn't spoil it is enough.
Deployers who publish AI-generated text to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose it, unless a person has reviewed it and someone holds editorial responsibility.

Deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems must inform the people exposed, and all these disclosures must be clear and given at the latest at the first interaction or exposure.

These duties are in Article 50 and, in the Act as published, apply from 2 August 2026; proposed changes could affect some timings, and a code of practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content was in preparation, so check the current position.

lab.title: Write the transparency measures for a product
lab.goal: Decide which transparency duties apply to three features of a fictional travel company's app, who is responsible for each, and draft the disclosures.
setup: A document or a sheet of paper
The scenario: an EU travel company's app has the three features in the first step

steps.do: Read the three features.
steps.code:
F1. A booking assistant chatbot, built by the company on another firm's general-purpose AI model through an API, offered under the company's brand.
F2. An image feature that lets users create realistic pictures of themselves at holiday destinations, built by the company on another firm's image-generation model.
F3. The marketing team uses AI to draft news articles on travel safety for the company's blog; an editor reviews and signs off each one.

steps.do: For each feature, name the company's role (provider, deployer or both) and the duties in Article 50 that apply, or why none do.
Under the heading Chatbot notice, write the first message F1 shows users, in plain words.

For F2, describe how outputs will be marked in a machine-readable way (for example, metadata or a watermark; C2PA content credentials are one open standard for provenance metadata) and whether a visible label is needed when users share pictures that could pass as real photos.
For F3, decide whether a disclosure is needed, given the editor's review and sign-off, and what the company must be able to show if asked.
List two things the company should ask the model providers for, to support its own compliance.

checks.text: The chatbot notice tells users clearly, at the start, that they're talking to an AI system.
F2's outputs are marked in a machine-readable way, as a provider duty.
F2's realistic pictures are treated as possible deep fakes that need a disclosure.
F3 uses the exception for human review and editorial responsibility correctly, with records to show it.
Each feature names the company's role, provider or deployer.
Questions for the model providers are included, such as documentation and support for marking outputs.

lab.submit: Paste your role and duty analysis for F1 to F3, your Chatbot notice, your marking and labelling plan for F2, your F3 decision and your two requests to the model providers.
hints: The company is the provider of F1 and F2, the systems it built and offers under its brand, even though other firms provide the models inside them.
Deep fake disclosure is a deployer duty; think about who generates and publishes the pictures, the user or the company, and how the app can help.

modules.title: The GDPR, other frameworks and your compliance programme
modules.summary: How the AI Act works alongside the GDPR, how the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 can structure your work, and how to build a compliance programme that keeps up with a changing timeline.

lessons.title: How the AI Act fits with the GDPR
objectives: Explain how the AI Act and the GDPR apply together
Map the AI Act's roles and assessments to the GDPR's
key_points: The AI Act doesn't replace the GDPR: whenever an AI system processes personal data, in training or in use, the GDPR applies too, with its own principles, legal bases and rights.
The roles differ: a provider or deployer under the AI Act may be a controller or processor under the GDPR, and an organisation needs to work out both for each system.

Training or using AI on personal data needs a lawful basis under the GDPR; the European Data Protection Board's Opinion 28/2024 discusses when legitimate interests can serve and when a model can be considered anonymous.

The GDPR's rules on solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, in Article 22, sit alongside the AI Act's duties to inform people and its right to an explanation for some high-risk decisions.
A data protection impact assessment under the GDPR and a fundamental rights impact assessment under the AI Act overlap, and the Act lets the second complement the first, so plan them together.
The AI Act allows providers of high-risk systems to process special categories of personal data, such as ethnic origin, where strictly necessary to detect and correct bias, with strict safeguards.

lessons.title: Beyond the EU: NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and international principles
objectives: Describe the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001
Use frameworks to support compliance in several jurisdictions
key_points: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework, published by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology in January 2023, is voluntary and organises AI risk work into four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.
NIST also publishes a Playbook of suggested actions, and profiles for particular uses, including a Generative AI Profile released in 2024.

ISO/IEC 42001, published in 2023, sets requirements for an AI management system: policies, roles, risk and impact assessment, controls and continual improvement, in the style of other ISO management standards, and organisations can be certified against it.

Related standards include ISO/IEC 23894 on AI risk management; the AI Act relies on harmonised European standards, being developed by CEN and CENELEC, which will give a presumption of conformity once published.

International frameworks include the OECD AI Principles and the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, the first international treaty on AI, opened for signature in 2024.
Frameworks don't replace legal obligations, but one well-run management system can produce much of the evidence that several laws, regulators and customers ask for.

lessons.title: Building a compliance programme
objectives: Plan an AI Act compliance programme from inventory to monitoring
Keep a programme current as guidance and timelines change
key_points: Start with an inventory of every AI system you build, buy or use, then classify each one (prohibited, high-risk, transparency duties, general-purpose model or minimal risk) and record your role for it.
Stop any prohibited practice at once, then run a gap analysis for high-risk systems and transparency duties: what the Act requires, what you already do, and who will close each gap by when.
Assign ownership: an accountable executive, a group that brings together legal, data protection, security, product and HR, and a clear sign-off for new AI uses.
Build in AI literacy training suited to each role, checks and contract terms for vendors, documentation, human oversight procedures, incident reporting and monitoring in use.
Reuse what exists: your GDPR programme, security and quality management systems, and frameworks such as ISO/IEC 42001 can carry much of the work.

Track change: the staged timeline, guidelines, codes of practice, harmonised standards and proposed amendments all affect what's needed and when, so check official sources, such as EUR-Lex and the Commission's AI Act pages, on a regular schedule.

project.title: An AI Act compliance plan for an HR-technology company
project.brief: A fictional HR-technology company of 300 staff, based in the EU, has asked for a compliance plan. It sells a CV-screening and candidate-ranking product, built on its own models, to employers across the EU. It's piloting an add-on that infers employees' emotions from their webcams during video calls, to give managers a team mood score. It offers a chatbot for candidates on clients' career sites, built on another firm's general-purpose AI model through an API. Internally, it uses a vendor's tool that monitors its own staff's productivity and flags low performers for review. Its marketing team makes blog illustrations with an image generator, and its finance team calculates commissions in a spreadsheet with fixed rules. Write the plan: classify every system and the company's role for it, say what must happen to anything prohibited, analyse the gaps for the high-risk systems as provider and as deployer, set out the transparency measures, explain how the GDPR applies alongside the Act, and design the governance and programme that will keep the company compliant. Describe obligations by stage rather than relying on fixed future dates, and say where the company should check the current timeline.
deliverables: An AI inventory: each system's classification, the company's role and the article or annex relied on
Immediate actions for any prohibited practice
A gap analysis for the high-risk product (as provider) and the staff-monitoring tool (as deployer)
Transparency measures for the chatbot and the image generator
A GDPR section: lawful bases, impact assessments and automated decisions
A programme plan: owners, AI literacy, vendor management, monitoring, incident reporting, and how the company will track the staged timeline

rubric.name: Classification and roles
rubric.description: Every system is classified correctly with reasons: the emotion add-on as prohibited, the screening product and the staff-monitoring tool as high-risk under Annex III, the chatbot under Article 50, and the commission spreadsheet as not an AI system; roles are right.

rubric.name: Prohibited practice handled
rubric.description: The emotion-recognition pilot is stopped, with clear actions on data already collected and on communication with clients.

rubric.name: High-risk gap analysis
rubric.description: Provider duties (risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, oversight, accuracy, conformity assessment, registration, post-market monitoring) and deployer duties are analysed with owners and actions.

rubric.name: Transparency and GDPR
rubric.description: Disclosures and output marking are appropriate; GDPR roles, lawful bases and impact assessments are identified, including a DPIA for monitoring staff.

rubric.name: Programme and governance
rubric.description: The programme names owners, training, vendor terms, monitoring and incident processes, and reuses existing frameworks sensibly.

rubric.name: Timeline and sources
rubric.description: Obligations are described by stage, future dates aren't treated as settled, and official sources to check are named.

project.submit: Paste your compliance plan, with the inventory as a table at the start.
